findings.headline: Bradford proposes raising council tax premiums on homes empty and unfurnished for over 5 years and over 10 years to the maximum permitted levels from 1 April 2027

The proposed premium is 200% for empty and unfurnished homes over 5 years but under 10 years, giving a total charge of 300% of normal council tax, and 300% for homes over 10 years, giving a total charge of 400%. The paper says the primary objective of the premiums is behavioural rather than financial, and it gives no estimate of the income effect.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council considering the same premium levers will see that Bradford is moving to the statutory maximum, and the paper gives no yield figure to benchmark against.
findings.figures: Current premium: 100% for both categories; proposed premium: 200% (total charge 300%) for over 5 years but under 10 years; 300% (total charge 400%) for over 10 years
findings.quote: The proposal will mean that owners of these properties will pay increased charges from 1st April 2027. Currently the premium for both categories is 100% so this proposal represents an increase.

findings.matters: Procurement thresholds set the point at which Procurement Act rules apply, so peers using the same figures can check their own tables against them.

findings.matters: Other administering authorities in the LGPS will be adjusting to the same Act and pooling requirements.
findings.quote: incorporate current requirements relating to asset pooling through Northern LGPS Limited

findings.quote: The sections relating to Partnerships, Joint Working and Council-owned Companies have been removed.

findings.figures: one-month period (replaced)

findings.detail: The paper reports strengthened reserve management provisions at paragraphs 5.45 to 5.53 (pages 37 to 38). It says the controls cover the withdrawal of funds from reserves and their annual review.

findings.quote: Clearer controls around withdrawal of funds from reserves and annual review arrangements.

findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare these thresholds and approval routes with their own virement rules.

findings.matters: A council that loses its partial exemption headroom can lose recovery of all its exempt-attributable VAT, so a finance director here or at a peer council needs to know both the current position and the size of the exposure.

findings.headline: £22.988m levy payment misclassified in draft accounts; required reclassification and prior-year adjustment

findings.paper_title: Doc O - Financial Statements 2025-26 for GAC 24 September 2026 V2.0
findings.headline: The Local Government Pension Scheme funded surplus of £871 million cannot be recognised on the balance sheet due to accounting restrictions.
findings.detail: The LGPS funded scheme has liabilities of £2.2bn and assets of £3.1bn, producing a surplus of £871m driven by actuarial gains from improved financial assumptions. However, IAS 19 accounting standards restrict recognition of this surplus through an asset ceiling mechanism, resulting in no net pension asset shown in the council's balance sheet.
findings.matters: While off-balance-sheet, a lender would assess the council's true pension position. The surplus improves the council's financial standing if realised, but the asset ceiling means this could reverse if investment returns fall or liabilities increase.
findings.figures: £871 million unrecognised surplus, £2.2 billion liabilities, £3.1 billion assets
findings.quote: However, accounting standards impose a restriction on the amount of surplus that can be recognised on the Council's balance sheet (known as the asset ceiling), as determined by the Council's actuary. In 2025–26, the asset ceiling restricted recognition of this surplus, resulting in no net pension asset being reported in the Balance Sheet.

findings.matters: Post-balance-sheet events affecting the council's reserves position change its true financial standing as of the reporting date and are material to a lender's assessment.
findings.figures: £4.9 million abortive costs
findings.quote: A post balance sheet event has been recognised following the Executive Decision in July 2026 not to proceed with the Square Lane capital project. As a result of this decision, £4.9m of abortive costs recognised on the Balance Sheet at the reporting date would have been charged to revenue expenditure had the decision been known at that date.

findings.paper_title: Doc O - Financial Statements 2025-26 for GAC 24 September 2026 V2.0
findings.headline: The Council's revenue outturn shows a £113 million overspend funded through government Capitalisation Direction.
findings.detail: The overspend was £14m better than initially forecast, but the council remains dependent on government financing to close its budget gap. This represents a significant operating deficit that is not being met from the council's own revenues.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can operate sustainably on its own revenues, or whether it requires continuing government bailout financing to manage budget shortfalls.
findings.figures: £113 million overspend, £14 million reduction from initial forecast
findings.quote: The revenue outturn for 2025–26 reflects an overspend of £113 million, which has been funded through the Capitalisation Direction (CD). This represents a £14million reduction compared to the initial forecast.

findings.paper_title: Doc N - WYPF Audit Completion Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Auditor anticipates unqualified opinion despite identifying material misstatements, as management adjusted actual errors but left extrapolated errors unadjusted.
findings.detail: Despite identifying £60.9m in level 3 valuation errors and £30.1m in level 1 errors, the auditor expects to issue a clean unqualified opinion (pending completion of outstanding procedures). Management's approach of adjusting actual known errors while leaving extrapolated errors unadjusted has been accepted as sufficient to address audit findings.
findings.matters: A clean audit opinion provides assurance that the reported fund valuations, while containing identified errors, are not materially misstated overall and that management has taken appropriate corrective action.
findings.figures: Unqualified opinion anticipated, subject to outstanding audit work
findings.quote: At the time of issuing this report and subject to the satisfactory conclusion of our remaining audit work, we anticipate issuing an unqualified opinion, without modification,.

findings.paper_title: Doc N - WYPF Audit Completion Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Level 1 investments (readily-valued assets) contained £30.1m extrapolated overstatement, indicating valuation issues span multiple asset categories.
findings.detail: Testing of Level 1 investments—assets valued using observable market data and thus easiest to verify—identified £14.6m actual understatement in the sample, extrapolating to £30.1m total overstatement. This remained unadjusted. Valuation errors across both subjective (Level 3) and objective (Level 1) asset categories suggest systematic problems in how the Fund prepares or reviews valuations.
findings.matters: Errors in objectively-valued assets suggest the valuation process has systematic weaknesses beyond timing or methodology differences, affecting confidence in overall reported asset values.
findings.figures: £30,124k unadjusted extrapolated overstatement, £14,651k actual error in tested sample
findings.quote: The total extrapolated error is an overstatement of £30,124k.

findings.paper_title: Doc N - WYPF Audit Completion Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Investment transaction values revised upward by £842.4m after initial transaction report proved to contain inaccurate information.
findings.detail: The initial transaction report supporting investment purchases and sales contained errors. Auditor testing found supporting evidence did not match reported values, prompting a complete revision. The revised report increased both purchases and sales values materially. This indicates data quality or internal control issues in transaction recording.
findings.matters: A large restatement of investment transaction values suggests systematic issues in the Fund's data systems or transaction controls, creating risk that other recorded transactions may be similarly misstated.
findings.figures: £842.4m combined increase to purchases and sales values
findings.quote: The initial detailed transaction report to support the Fund's purchases and sales transactions contained inaccurate information. In testing a sample of transactions we established the supporting evidence did not agree to the value included in the report. A revised report was subsequently produced which resulted in a large increase in the value of purchases and sales.

findings.paper_title: Doc N - WYPF Audit Completion Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Level 3 investments worth £4.3bn contained £60.9m actual valuation error, with a further £30.3m estimated error remaining unadjusted.
findings.detail: The Fund's most subjectively-valued investments (20.1% of net investment assets) showed significant differences between recorded values and fund manager valuations. Timing differences meant fund managers had more current valuations available after draft accounts were prepared.
findings.matters: Pension fund asset valuations determine the council's pension liability position and contribution requirements; material valuation uncertainties affect financial forecasting.
findings.figures: £4,322m level 3 assets, £60,978k adjusted, £30,325k unadjusted extrapolated error, 20.1% of net investment assets, materiality £225.1m
findings.quote: The pension fund have adjusted the financial statements by the actual known error of £60,978k, leaving a residual unadjusted extrapolated misstatement of £30,325k.

findings.paper_title: Doc N - Covering Report External Audit Completions 2025-26 for GAC 24 September 2026
findings.headline: Audit opinion is subject to resolution of outstanding queries, with unqualified opinion anticipated rather than final.
findings.detail: The auditor states they anticipate issuing an unqualified audit opinion on the council's 2025-26 financial statements, but this is explicitly conditional on completion of outstanding audit queries. This indicates the audit process remains unfinished at the point of reporting to the committee.
findings.matters: A lender requires certainty that accounts have received a clean, final audit opinion. An anticipated opinion contingent on unresolved audit queries leaves the final position uncertain.

findings.paper_title: Doc M - Sufficiency update and capital programme exec report Sept 2026
findings.headline: Funded early years provision take-up significantly below national average in disadvantaged areas
findings.detail: 'Terrific Twos' (2-year-olds) take-up at 65.1% vs national average 75.1%. Universal funded early education (3-4 year-olds) at 85.5% vs national 90%. Report notes significant gaps in most disadvantaged areas despite targeted support campaigns.
findings.matters: Below-target take-up of heavily-promoted childcare entitlements in disadvantaged areas suggests delivery or uptake challenges; may indicate local market difficulties or lower-than-expected demand, affecting viability of expanded provision.
findings.figures: 'Terrific Twos' 65.1% vs 75.1% national; FEE 85.5% vs 90% national; an increase of only 0.4% autumn to spring term

findings.paper_title: Doc M - Sufficiency update and capital programme exec report Sept 2026
findings.headline: Secondary schools forecast to have high surplus places 2028-2030 as lower primary cohorts progress; current intakes already lowest in several years
findings.detail: Secondary intakes September 2026 are lowest for several years. Forecasts show high levels of Year 7 surplus 2028-2030 as smaller primary school cohorts work through. Surpluses range from -56 to -589 places depending on planning area by 2030.
findings.matters: Secondary schools currently at capacity will face significant budget pressure and viability challenges from 2028 onwards; this creates forward-looking school consolidation decisions and workforce planning challenges not yet reflected in immediate budgets.
findings.figures: Lowest secondary intakes in several years (Sept 2026); 2030 forecasts show surpluses: -56 to -589 places across planning areas
findings.quote: However as with primary school places, the decline into Year 7 at secondary school has started to decline, with September 2026 intakes being the lowest for several years. Between 2028 and 2030 the forecasts indicate high levels of surplus in Y7 as the lower numbers come through from primary schools.

findings.paper_title: Doc M - Sufficiency update and capital programme exec report Sept 2026
findings.headline: Primary school consolidation ongoing: 1,067 places removed 2021-2027; further 330 places still need to be cut
findings.detail: Birth numbers declined ~1,000 since 2015. Council has already cut 1,067 reception class places through Published Admission Number (PAN) reductions; forecasts indicate 330 further places must still be removed. Bradford currently carries 12% surplus, aiming for 5-8% sustainable level.
findings.matters: Ongoing requirement to reduce primary school capacity signals structural financial pressure on schools with falling rolls; continuing consolidation implies difficult decisions on school viability, potential closures/mergers, and workforce implications.
findings.figures: 1,067 reception places reduced 2021-2027; 330 more places still required; current 12% surplus vs 5-8% target
findings.quote: Between 2021 and 2027 there will have been 1067 reception class places reduced across the district, to address the decline and support schools to be sustainable. Forecasts indicate that a further 11 forms of entry (330 reception class places) are still required to be taken out of the admissions system

findings.paper_title: Doc M - Sufficiency update and capital programme exec report Sept 2026
findings.headline: Out-of-authority SEND placements cost £43.5k more per place than locally-created provision, straining DSG High Needs Block
findings.detail: Growing numbers of children are placed in independent sector provision due to shortage of local places. Each out-of-authority placement costs significantly more than locally-created specialist places, creating uncontrolled financial pressure on the DSG. Council is investing capital to create local capacity as mitigation.
findings.matters: Until local SEND capacity is built out, the DSG remains under pressure from expensive independent placements; this creates a forced capital investment requirement to avoid ever-rising DSG costs; per-place cost differential represents material financial exposure.
findings.figures: Independent placements cost £43.5k per place more than local provision; Bradford creating places at £40.5k average vs national average £85k
findings.quote: the cost of locally created places to the DSG is significantly lower on average than the cost of placements especially in the independent sector, that are £43,500 per place on average higher.

findings.paper_title: Doc M - Sufficiency update and capital programme exec report Sept 2026
findings.headline: EHCP numbers up 21% in 18 months to 9,064, driving both capital and revenue pressures on constrained DSG High Needs Block
findings.detail: 9,064 children aged 0-25 with EHCPs as of July 2026, up from 7,480 in January 2025 — a rise of 1,600 (21%) in just 18 months. School-aged population (5-16) increased identically: 5,396 to 6,572. This explosive growth is creating overcapacity in schools and driving requirement for continuous capital expansion.
findings.matters: Rapidly growing EHCP demand drives both major capital spending requirements and ongoing revenue costs from the DSG High Needs Block; this is a structural demand shift that affects the council's medium-term financial planning and sustainability.
findings.figures: 9,064 children (July 2026) vs 7,480 (January 2025); school-aged 6,572 vs 5,396; 21% growth in 18 months
findings.quote: As of July 2026, there were 9064 children and young people aged 0-25 years with an EHCP. Comparing to the figures in January 2025, this represents a rise of nearly 1600 (21%) over the 18-month period.

findings.committee: West Yorkshire Pension Fund Advisory Panel
findings.paper_title: Agenda item 8 Pensions Administration Report
findings.headline: SCAPE discount rate increase has suspended critical pension calculations pending new actuarial factors, extending timelines by up to six months
findings.detail: The SCAPE discount rate increased from CPI + 1.7% to CPI + 2.0% effective 19 May 2026. This has required suspension of non-Club transfers, aggregation calculations, and divorce cash equivalent valuations until updated actuarial factors are issued. Early and late retirement factors are expected within six weeks, with remaining factors issued over six months.
findings.matters: Suspended transfer-out processing creates bottlenecks affecting member and employer experience; delays in member valuations disrupt retirement planning for members and inter-fund administration
findings.figures: Discount rate increase: CPI + 1.7% to CPI + 2.0%; factor delays: 6 weeks to 6 months
findings.quote: The revised SCAPE discount rate applies from 19 May 2026 and has increased from CPI + 1.7% to CPI + 2.0%. As a result, we had to suspend some calculations until new factors are issued. These include certain non-Club transfers and aggregation calculations, as well as all cash equivalent values (CEVs) for divorce.

findings.committee: West Yorkshire Pension Fund Advisory Panel
findings.paper_title: Agenda item 8 Pensions Administration Report
findings.headline: Internal audit rated life certificate controls as only partially effective, finding multiple risks not effectively managed
findings.detail: Bradford's Internal Audit team audited life certificate administration and determined that the control environment is only partially effective. Multiple examined risks were found to not be effectively managed, and the audit concluded that controls would benefit from significant improvement to support key business objectives. Three recommendations were made and implemented.
findings.matters: Weakness in life certificate controls creates risk of overpayments to deceased pensioners; as a material process in pension administration, control failures here expose Bradford to financial loss and regulatory scrutiny
findings.figures: Three audit recommendations made and implemented
findings.quote: It is audit's opinion that the standard of control of identified risks in the system is partially effective. The audit review has determined that a number of the risks examined are not effectively managed. The control environment would benefit from significant improvement to support the achievement of key business objectives.

findings.committee: West Yorkshire Pension Fund Advisory Panel
findings.paper_title: Agenda item 8 Pensions Administration Report
findings.headline: WYPF will breach McCloud statutory guidance deadline of 31 August 2026 for retrospective pension amendments due to software development not received from Civica
findings.detail: The McCloud implementation statutory guidance requires all retrospective amendments to members' pensions to be concluded by 31 August 2026. Civica, the pensions administration system provider, has not delivered the necessary software development to enable retrospective calculations. As a result, WYPF will be in breach of the guidance and must report this to the Pensions Regulator. The formal recommendation is that this breach is reported to TPR.
findings.matters: Breaching Pensions Regulator requirements can result in fines and regulatory action; as Bradford hosts WYPF, this compliance failure reflects on Bradford's governance and ability to manage complex regulatory obligations
findings.figures: Deadline 31 August 2026; software update still not received as of report date (27 August 2026)
findings.quote: The McCloud implementation statutory guidance states that all retrospective amendments to members' pensions should be concluded by 31 August 2026. Civica clients have not received the software development to enable them to do the retrospective calculations. As a result WYPF will be in breach of the guidance and should report this to the Pensions Regulator ('TPR').

findings.paper_title: Doc E - Business Rates and Council Tax Collection
findings.headline: Five-tier business rates multiplier from April 2026 reduces retail, hospitality and leisure rates by 23%: small business 49.9p to 38.2p, standard 55.5p to 43.0p
findings.detail: From April 2026, five new multiplier rate bands replaced the previous two-tier system. Rates for retail, hospitality and leisure businesses were substantially cut: small business multiplier fell from 49.9p to 38.2p (23% reduction); standard RHL from 55.5p to 43.0p (23% reduction). This follows a simultaneous property revaluation, compounding revenue reduction.
findings.matters: Substantial reduction in multiplier rates for economically distressed business sectors reduces projected business rates income and creates budgetary pressure in the forward year.

findings.paper_title: Doc E - Business Rates and Council Tax Collection
findings.headline: Successful business rates appeals created £2.96m budget hit in single financial year
findings.detail: In 2025/26, successful appeals against rateable values resulted in retrospective adjustments totalling £2.96m. These adjustments can be backdated over several years and have material impact on the council's budget position. The council manages this through provisions in its budget process but volatility reduces predictability.
findings.matters: Large appeals-driven revenue adjustments create unpredictability in the council's tax income and require reserve provisions to absorb impacts; this reduces financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £2.96m in retrospective adjustments in 2025/26; adjustments can be backdated over several years
findings.quote: In 2025/26, successful appeals by businesses have resulted in retrospective adjustments in liability totalling £2.96m.

findings.paper_title: Doc E - Business Rates and Council Tax Collection
findings.headline: Council tax collection rate fell to 93.54% following 9.99% tax increase
findings.detail: In-year council tax collection declined from 94.04% to 93.54% in 2025/26 despite a 9.99% council tax rise that increased the total liability from £308m to £341m. The paper attributes collection difficulties to the large tax increase, new charges on empty properties from April 2025, and poverty affecting residents' ability to pay.
findings.matters: A large tax increase producing a collection rate decline rather than improvement indicates residents are reaching the limit of affordability; this signals underlying financial stress and suggests collection will remain difficult.
findings.figures: Council Tax liability 2025/26: £341m; 2024/25: £308m (increase of £33m or 10.7%); 9.99% council tax rise; collection rate fell to 93.54% from 94.04%
findings.quote: Council Tax in year collection for 2025/26 was 93.54% which is 0.5% down on the previous year (Table 4) Factors affecting collection include the 9.99% Council Tax rise in 2025/26, increases in charges on empty properties which came into force in April 2025 and wider factors affecting collection such as poverty in the district.

findings.paper_title: Doc E - Business Rates and Council Tax Collection
findings.headline: Business rates collection rate declined to 95.28%, lowest in five-year trend
findings.detail: In-year business rates collection fell from 96.45% in 2024/25 to 95.28% in 2025/26—a drop of 1.17 percentage points. The paper attributes this to increased collection amounts (£138m vs £128m), reduced reliefs, and ongoing economic pressures particularly affecting retail, hospitality and leisure businesses.
findings.matters: Declining collection efficiency reduces cash available to the council and indicates collection effort is not keeping pace with growing arrears; this impacts cash flow and financial planning.
findings.figures: 2025/26 collection: 95.28%; 2024/25: 96.45%; 2023/24: 97.26%—a three-year downward trend
findings.quote: Business Rates in year collection for 2025/26 was 95.28% which is 1.17% down on the previous year (Table 1). Factors affecting collection include the increased amount to collect, decreases in reliefs and the ongoing economic situation which affects businesses (particularly the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors).

findings.paper_title: Doc E - Business Rates and Council Tax Collection
findings.headline: Outstanding business rates arrears more than doubled to £5.3m whilst 463 businesses face insolvency or strike-off
findings.detail: Business rates debt outstanding at end March 2026 reached £5.336m, doubling from £2.851m a year earlier. This occurs amid 350 companies identified at proposal to strike-off stage and 113 in liquidation, administration or insolvency, indicating acute economic distress in the local business environment affecting payment capacity.
findings.matters: Doubling of business rates arrears combined with high insolvency rates indicates the local business base is under severe stress; this threatens future collection and reflects economic deterioration affecting the council's revenue base.
findings.figures: Outstanding debt 2025/26: £5,336k vs 2024/25: £2,851k; 350 companies at proposal to strike off; 113 in insolvency/administration/liquidation
findings.quote: Active Business Rates data is matched to Company House records monthly, and the latest report shows that there are 350 cases at proposal to strike off and 113 cases identified where the ratepayer is in liquidation, administration or other form of insolvency.

findings.detail: Council tax debt outstanding at end March 2026 reached £20.591m, more than double the £9.949m owed a year earlier.
